13:I[9227,["809","static/chunks/809-a74e063132212cdb.js","714","static/chunks/714-e58065388e176c6d.js","690","static/chunks/app/verse/%5Bid%5D/page-179c881197ecc822.js"],"default"]
8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":20,"verseId":3,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Cause and Effect (Saṃbhava)","totalVerses":24,"verseData":{"id":"v20_3","number":3,"title":"If the Effect Pre-Exists, It Should Be Perceivable — But It Isn't","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"If the effect is in the combination Of causes and conditions, Then it should be grasped in the combination. But it is not grasped in the combination."},"philosophy":{"insight":"The EMPIRICAL test: if the effect inherently pre-exists in the cause-combination (v.1's position), we should be able to PERCEIVE it there before it arises. But we don't — we can't taste the cake in the raw batter. The pre-existence claim fails empirically, not just logically.","madhyamaka":"Phala sāmagrī-gata cet (if the effect is in the combination), sāmagrī-madhye gṛhyeta (it should be grasped/perceived in the combination). Na ca sāmagrī-madhye gṛhyate (but it is not grasped in the combination). This is a pramāṇa (epistemic) argument: inherent pre-existence should be observable, but it isn't.","quantum":"Unobservability of quantum potentiality: the wave function (containing all possible outcomes) can't be directly observed — only the actual outcome after measurement is perceivable. If outcomes pre-existed in the wave function, they should be detectable. But they're not. Like v.3: pre-existing effects should be perceivable but aren't.","bridge":"Both v.3 and quantum potentiality show that the \"pre-existing\" entity can't be empirically found. QM: you can't observe which outcome will occur before measurement. V.3: you can't perceive the effect before it arises. Both: pre-existence fails the empirical test.","accessible":"Look at flour, eggs, and sugar before mixing. Can you see the cake? Taste it? Touch it? No. If the cake pre-existed in the ingredients, you should be able to detect it. But you can't. The cake genuinely arises through baking — it doesn't just become visible.","twoTruths":"Conventionally: we know the ingredients CAN produce cake (potential). Ultimately: the cake isn't inherently there — it's not perceivable in the ingredients. Conventional potential ≠ inherent pre-existence.","commonMisconception":"NOT saying ingredients have no potential for cake. CONVENTIONAL potential is acknowledged. What's denied is INHERENT pre-existence — the idea that the cake is actually, detectably present in the ingredients before baking."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Unobservability of Quantum Potentiality","score":62,"strength":"Medium","explanation":"The wave function contains \"all possibilities\" but none can be observed before measurement. Like v.3: if the effect pre-existed, it should be perceivable — but it isn't. Both: pre-existence fails the empirical test.","caveat":"Quantum unobservability is a physics principle. V.3 is a philosophical argument. The parallel is about the empirical invisibility of supposedly \"pre-existing\" entities."},"animation":{"visualBridge":"A magnifying glass examining a cause-combination (ingredients), searching for the effect (cake). Nothing found — the effect isn't perceivable in the causes. Caption: \"If it's there, we should find it. We don't.\"","educationalGoal":"User sees the empirical argument: pre-existence should be detectable. It isn't. Therefore: the effect doesn't inherently pre-exist in the cause."},"deeperDive":[{"q":"Why should pre-existence be perceivable?","a":"If something inherently EXISTS, it should be findable/perceivable by appropriate cognition. That's what \"exists\" means in the inherent sense — it's there, from its own side, independently. If it's inherently there, some mode of cognition should be able to detect it.","realLifeExample":"If there's a cat in the box, you should be able to detect it (hear it, see it, weigh the box). If the cat can't be detected by ANY means, claiming it \"inherently exists\" in the box is unjustified."},{"q":"Isn't the effect there \"in potential\"?","a":"Conventional potential is fine — we acknowledge that flour has the POTENTIAL for cake. But \"potential\" ≠ \"inherent pre-existence.\" Potential is a conventional designation about future possibilities. Inherent pre-existence claims the effect is ACTUALLY there, right now, in the cause. V.3 tests this stronger claim.","realLifeExample":"A block of marble has the \"potential\" for any sculpture — but no specific sculpture actually pre-exists in it. \"Potential\" is about future possibility, not present inherent existence."},{"q":"How does this empirical argument complement the logical one (v.1)?","a":"V.1: logical argument — pre-existence makes \"arising\" meaningless. V.3: empirical argument — pre-existence should be perceivable but isn't. Together: pre-existence fails both logically (v.1) and empirically (v.3). Two independent arguments converging on the same conclusion.","realLifeExample":"Two ways to disprove \"there's gold in this rock\": (1) Logic: if gold were there, the rock would be heavier (it isn't). (2) Empirical: we tested it and found no gold. Both arguments support the conclusion independently."},{"q":"What is the relationship between v.3 and pramāṇa (epistemology)?","a":"Pramāṇa means \"valid cognition\" — the means by which we know things. V.3 says: no valid cognition finds the effect in the causes before it arises. If no pramāṇa can detect the pre-existing effect, we have no grounds for asserting its inherent pre-existence. The epistemology doesn't support the metaphysics.","realLifeExample":"A scientist claims a new particle exists. Others say: \"Show us the evidence.\" If no experiment can detect it, the claim is unjustified. V.3 applies this empirical standard to inherent pre-existence."},{"q":"How does quantum mechanics parallel this?","a":"In QM, the wave function contains \"all possibilities\" (like pre-existence of all outcomes). But you can NEVER observe which outcome will occur before measurement. The pre-existing outcome is empirically undetectable. Like v.3: if the effect pre-exists, it should be findable — but it isn't.","realLifeExample":"Schrödinger's cat: is it alive or dead before you open the box? You can't detect its state until you look. The \"pre-existing\" state is empirically inaccessible. V.3 makes the same point about cause-effect."},{"q":"What is the philosophical impact?","a":"V.3 shifts the debate from pure logic to EVIDENCE. Even if someone isn't convinced by v.1's logical argument, v.3 provides an empirical challenge: show me the effect in the causes before it arises. If you can't, your claim of inherent pre-existence is unfounded.","deeper":"V.3 is particularly powerful because it challenges the opponent to DEMONSTRATE pre-existence, not just argue for it. This is an empirical/epistemic move that complements the purely logical arguments. In Buddhist epistemology, claims about existence must be supported by valid cognition (pramāṇa). V.3 says: no valid cognition supports pre-existence. This is a move that resonates with modern empiricism: extraordinary claims (the effect already exists in the cause) require extraordinary evidence (perceivability). The evidence is absent; the claim is unjustified."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"Can you perceive the cake in the raw ingredients?","options":["A) Yes","B) No — and that's v.3's point. If the cake inherently pre-existed in the ingredients, you should be able to detect it there. But you can't. Therefore: the cake doesn't inherently pre-exist.","C) Only with special vision","D) The cake is hidden"],"correct":"B","explanation":"Pre-existence should be perceivable. It isn't. Therefore: no inherent pre-existence."},"intermediate":{"question":"How does v.3 complement v.1?","options":["A) It doesn't","B) V.1: LOGICAL argument (pre-existence makes arising meaningless). V.3: EMPIRICAL argument (pre-existence should be perceivable but isn't). Two independent arguments, same conclusion: inherent pre-existence fails.","C) They're the same","D) Only v.1 matters"],"correct":"B","explanation":"Logic (v.1) + empirics (v.3) = two independent refutations of pre-existence. Both converge on emptiness."},"advanced":{"question":"How does v.3 apply pramāṇa (valid cognition) to the pre-existence debate?","options":["A) No application","B) V.3 demands empirical evidence: if the effect inherently pre-exists, some valid cognition should detect it. None does. Claims of inherent pre-existence are epistemically unfounded — not supported by any mode of valid cognition.","C) Pramāṇa supports pre-existence","D) Epistemology is irrelevant"],"correct":"B","explanation":"No valid cognition detects pre-existing effects in causes. The epistemology doesn't support the metaphysics. Extraordinary claim, no evidence."}},"verseText":"If the effect is in the combination Of causes and conditions, Then it should be grasped in the combination. But it is not grasped in the combination.","madhyamakaConcept":"Phala sāmagrī-gata cet (if the effect is in the combination), sāmagrī-madhye gṛhyeta (it should be grasped/perceived in the combination). Na ca sāmagrī-madhye gṛhyate (but it is not grasped in the combination). This is a pramāṇa (epistemic) argument: inherent pre-existence should be observable, but it isn't.","quantumPhysicsParallel":"Unobservability of quantum potentiality: the wave function (containing all possible outcomes) can't be directly observed — only the actual outcome after measurement is perceivable. If outcomes pre-existed in the wave function, they should be detectable. But they're not. Like v.3: pre-existing effects should be perceivable but aren't."}},"isShowcase":false,"chapterId":20}]
